thread:
ryan (Customer): Hey team — after we moved the private connector behind our corp proxy, requests to Redwood's Private endpoint intermittently return 502s during the TLS handshake. Works from dev laptop but fails from app hosts behind proxy.

jamie (Support): Sorry you're hitting that, can you share a recent curl from an app host? Also which Private deployment region/VPC?

ryan (Customer): region: eu-west-1, private overlay VPC. From app host: `curl -v -x http://corp-proxy:8080 https://private.redwood.example/v1/models` -> shows CONNECT established then TLS handshake error: `alert handshake_failure` and `no shared cipher`.

maria (Eng): Can you paste the full curl output (verbosity) and the CONNECT negotiation? Interested if proxy is touching SNI or inserting headers.

ryan (Customer): Full: 
```
*   Trying 10.1.2.5:8080... connected
* Connected to corp-proxy (10.1.2.5) port 8080 (#0)
> CONNECT private.redwood.example:443 HTTP/1.1
> Host: private.redwood.example:443
> Proxy-Connection: Keep-Alive
> User-Agent: curl/7.68.0
> Accept: */*
< HTTP/1.1 200 Connection established
< Proxy-Agent: Corp-GW/2.1
< X-Forwarded-For: 10.10.10.10

* ALPN, server did not agree to a protocol
* TLSv1.3 (OUT), TLS handshake, Client hello (1):
* TLSv1.3 (IN), TLS alert, server hello (level: fatal, description: handshake failure)
* error:1409442E:SSL routines:ssl3_read_bytes:tlsv1 alert handshake failure
```

noah (NetOps): That Proxy-Agent header stands out. Our corp proxy mutates CONNECT replies and injects `Proxy-Agent` and `X-Forwarded-For`. That shouldn't break raw TLS unless it re-writes SNI or terminates TLS (MITM). Do you see any TLS cert presented?

ryan (Customer): No cert chain printed from curl. From tcpdump on host we see a TLS ClientHello from host to proxy, but after CONNECT 200 the bytes go through. Proxy returns 200 and then some SYN resets after handshake failure.

maria (Eng): Two hypotheses: 1) Proxy is doing TLS interception (MITM) and presenting its own cert, causing handshake failure because client expects Redwood cert; or 2) Proxy rewrites the CONNECT target or strips SNI, causing Redwood's edge to select wrong cert/ALPN and drop.

jamie (Support): Quick check: can you run `openssl s_client -connect private.redwood.example:443 -servername private.redwood.example -proxy corp-proxy:8080 -alpn h2` from the same host and paste output? That will show certs and SNI negotiation.

ryan (Customer): Run output: 
```
CONNECTED(00000003)\nwrite:errno=104\n139768215234304:error:1409E0E5:SSL routines:ssl3_write_bytes:ssl handshake failure:ssl/record/rec_layer_s3.c:1536:
---
No peer certificate available
---
SSL handshake has read 0 bytes and written 302 bytes
---
```

maria (Eng): That `No peer certificate available` after proxy 200 usually means the proxy accepted CONNECT but then injected something or blocked the raw bytes. Can you get a hex dump of the bytes after CONNECT? Also check proxy logs for `CONNECT private.redwood.example` and any ACL policy.

noah (NetOps): Confirmed with corp GW team: they have a policy that inspects CONNECTs to non-standard hostnames and will either MITM (terminate TLS) or, if the hostname is in an allowlist, do pure tunneling. Looks like private.redwood.example isn't in their allowlist and they attempt MITM with a custom TLS stack that doesn't handle TLS1.3 or SNI passthrough well.

ryan (Customer): Is there a suggested workaround? We can't change corp proxy rules easily.

maria (Eng): Workarounds: 1) Add private.redwood.example to the proxy's CONNECT allowlist so it doesn't MITM. 2) Use a dedicated egress host/VPN that bypasses corp proxy for the Redwood VPC (egress rule). 3) If you control the client, configure TLS to use older ciphers as a temporary measure (not recommended). Also check if proxy rewrites Host header in CONNECT reply — it should not.

jamie (Support): For immediate repro: can you try `curl --proxy-insecure -x http://corp-proxy:8080 https://private.redwood.example/v1/models -v` to see if proxy presents its own cert? It will still fail but may show cert details.

ryan (Customer): Tried `--proxy-insecure` same result; curl shows no cert. Proxy team provided a snippet from their logs: `CONNECT private.redwood.example:443 allowed -> MITM attempt using TLS-inspect-profile-legacy` and then `handshake failure: unsupported client hello extensions`.

maria (Eng): That log clinches it. Their TLS-inspect stack is incompatible (likely strips SNI or doesn't support latest extensions we use). Two action items for you and for us:
- Ryan / NetOps: request the proxy team to add private.redwood.example to the explicit CONNECT allowlist or enable SNI passthrough for that FQDN. If they must MITM, ask them to enable TLS1.3 and modern cipher suites and not to strip SNI.
- Maria / Eng: we'll add advice to our Private deploy docs about needed egress allowlist entries and a troubleshooting checklist for CONNECT/MITM. Also add a clear error code mapping when we detect missing client cert during handshake to surface better diagnostic to customers.

noah (NetOps): We'll open a ticket with Corp-GW. Quick question for Eng: can Redwood Private accept a fallback port like 8443 for customers behind restrictive proxies? If proxy policies allow non-443 tunnels differently it might help.

maria (Eng): We can consider exposing a dedicated egress-host endpoint on a configurable tcp port, but that requires customers to update their routing. Not ideal, but possible. We'll discuss feasibility with infra.

jamie (Support): I'll keep this thread open. Ryan, once your proxy team confirms allowlist addition, ping us and we'll validate. In the meantime, please attach any proxy logs showing `TLS-inspect-profile-legacy`.

ryan (Customer): Thanks — opening ticket with Corp-GW now and will update. Appreciate the quick triage. :pray:
